request.system:
You extract facts from a UK commercial/residential property sale brochure (e.g. an Acuitus or Allsop lot).
For each field return {"value": ..., "page": <page number>, "excerpt": "<short text copied EXACTLY, character for character, from that page>"} or null if the brochure does not state it.
The excerpt must be a verbatim substring of the page text (10-120 characters) that contains the value. Never infer, convert or calculate a value that is not printed.
Fields: address (string, without postcode), postcode (string), property_type (string, e.g. "Retail", "Office", "Residential flats"), price_gbp (number, guide or asking price in pounds), price_kind ("guide" | "asking" | null, not cited),
rent_pa_gbp (number, current gross rent per annum in pounds), yield_pct (number, e.g. 7.25), size_sqft (number, total floor area in square feet), tenure (string, e.g. "Freehold"), dwellings (integer, number of residential units, only if stated).
Return JSON with exactly these keys.

Buy each property directly
Direct ownership is the simplest route and keeps the pension fund's tax treatment closest to the assets,
with no company layer to run. The trade-off is that each residential property has to be bought and later sold
one by one, which means more transaction costs and paperwork on exit.

One UK SPV owns the portfolio
Holding the residential portfolio in one SPV lets the fund buy and sell it as a single package and could make
a later sale through a share transfer cheaper for a buyer. The trade-off is that a company holding dwellings
may face extra residential charges and corporate-level tax that the pension fund would not face holding
directly.

Fund (unit trust) owns the SPV

pension fund and makes it easier to bring in co-investors later. The trade-off is extra set-up cost, governance
and eligibility conditions that need to be met and kept up.
